name: The balanced plate — what each part is DOING
strand: Building a diet that fits your goals
scope: The plate model isn't arbitrary decoration; each section has a mechanical job. T1: on a plate of protein + vegetables + a smart carb + fat, the part your body uses to BUILD and repair itself (muscle, skin, hair) is the protein — meat, eggs, beans (not the bread or the oil). T2 (invert the wonder): a big green salad with NO oil on it barely gives you some of its vitamins — because vitamins A, D, E and K are fat-soluble, and fat is the truck that carries them in; the answer is the drizzle of oil/fat. T3: vegetables get to fill HALF the plate because they are the lowest-calorie section — mostly water and fiber (a cucumber is ~97% water), so you can eat a big satisfying volume for very few calories. T4: the difference between a 'smart' carb (oats, beans, a whole potato) and an 'empty' one (candy, white bread) is fiber — the smart carb releases its energy slowly. T4b (one model's choice): Harvard's Healthy Eating Plate pointedly does NOT count the potato as a vegetable and swaps the milk glass for a water glass, because a plain potato behaves like a fast starch, not a leafy vegetable.
source: Harvard T.H. Chan Nutrition Source (Healthy Eating Plate vs USDA MyPlate); Harvard Health 'Comparison of Healthy Eating Plate and MyPlate'; USDA MyPlate; NIH ODS fat-soluble vitamin fact sheets. Grokipedia attempted (403).
framing_note: Scene-led, food-anchored: every answer is a specific food or a food's job, never 'what is a balanced diet?'. The dinner-test payoff is T2 — the oil on the salad is what unlocks the salad's vitamins. ACCURACY RAIL: present the plate as a useful DEFAULT, not a law; do NOT inherit Harvard's blanket 'avoid red meat' framing (it conflicts with this bank's traditional-foods lean) — treat the potato-as-starch and water-not-milk choices as ONE model's reasoning, not settled truth. Keep red meat and whole-fat dairy neutral-to-positive.

name: Protein — the body's building blocks
strand: Building a diet that fits your goals
scope: Protein deepened from 'quick fuel' myth to the muscle-building signal. T1 (invert): your body can't stockpile protein the way it hoards fat — so it takes the protein you eat apart into smaller reusable units and rebuilds its own; those units are amino acids. T2: of the ~20 amino acids, 9 are 'essential' — the body genuinely cannot make them, so a food source must supply them or you run short. T3: a 'complete' protein has all nine essentials in good amounts — eggs, fish, meat and dairy do; most single plant foods are short one (rice is low in lysine, beans low in methionine), which is exactly why rice AND beans eaten together make a complete protein (they cover each other's gap). T4: growing kids and muscle-builders need MORE protein per pound of bodyweight than a sedentary adult — the famous 0.8 g/kg figure is a floor to avoid deficiency, not the target for building (athletes aim far higher); the tested idea is 'more for growth/training', not the number. T5 (payoff): one specific amino acid, leucine, is the 'GO' switch that tells muscle to start building — which is why leucine-rich foods like eggs and whey trigger more muscle-building than an equal gram-count of low-leucine plant protein.
source: Examine.com Protein Intake Guide; Harvard Health 'How much protein do you need'; StrengthLog protein-by-age; HealthyChildren.org teen-athlete protein; PMC8147948 (child protein requirements); Wikipedia (essential amino acids, complementary proteins, leucine/mTOR). Grokipedia attempted (403).
framing_note: Scene-led; answers are foods or the named nutrient (amino acids, leucine, rice+beans), never a definition shell. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (rice+beans complete each other) and T5 (leucine is the build-signal). ACCURACY RAIL: steel-man plant protein — the honest point is that plants CAN make a complete protein by combining, not that they're useless. The RDA number and 'mTOR' are context/distractors only, never the tested answer (banned minutiae).

name: Nutrient density — liver, nature's multivitamin
strand: Building a diet that fits your goals
scope: The most nutrition per calorie, built around the champion food. T1: 'empty calories' means energy with almost no vitamins or minerals — a can of soda; contrast a boiled egg of similar calories that is packed with nutrients (the concept: nutrition-per-calorie, not just calories). T2 (invert the wonder): ounce for ounce the single most nutrient-dense common food is an organ most kids never touch and old cultures treated as sacred and fed to pregnant mothers — liver. T3: liver's headline nutrient is vitamin A in the ready-to-use form (retinol) — one small serving holds roughly a week's worth, which is why you eat liver about once a week, not daily. T4 (payoff): you can actually get TOO much of that vitamin — Arctic explorers who ate polar-bear (or husky) liver got violently ill from vitamin A poisoning; the Inuit knew to avoid it. T5: nutrient density is about absorbability, not just amount — liver's iron is heme iron the body grabs easily, while spinach's iron is non-heme and partly locked up by the plant's own oxalates, so a small piece of liver beats a big bowl of spinach for usable iron (busting the Popeye idea). Also: in an egg it's the YOLK, not the white, that carries the choline, fat-soluble vitamins and minerals.
source: Nutrivore beef-liver nutrient profile; Healthline 'Why liver is a superfood'; NIH ODS Vitamin A (retinol, hypervitaminosis A); documented Arctic polar-bear-liver hypervitaminosis A cases; NIH ODS Iron (heme vs non-heme, oxalate inhibition). Grokipedia attempted (403).
framing_note: Scene-led, matter-of-fact about offal (never gory). Dinner-test payoff: T4 (polar-bear liver poisons you — too much vitamin A). ACCURACY RAILS: (1) vitamin A toxicity is real — DO NOT strawman the mainstream caution; the correct message is 'liver weekly, not daily'. (2) The Popeye 'misplaced-decimal' origin story is itself an unverified legend — do NOT teach it as fact; the true point is spinach iron is non-heme and poorly absorbed. Leans traditional-foods (steer toward organ/animal foods), so vision_mandated true; steel-man the 'limit organ meat' view via the toxicity angle.

name: Fats — what they do, and the seed-oil debate
strand: Building a diet that fits your goals
scope: From 'fat is the enemy' to the real modern argument. T2: fat is not the enemy — your brain is mostly fat (by dry weight), and dietary fat is what lets you absorb vitamins A, D, E and K; a truly fat-free diet starves the brain and blocks those vitamins. T3: fats come in families you can tell apart by behavior — saturated fats stay solid on the counter (butter, tallow, coconut), monounsaturated pours but firms in the fridge (olive oil), polyunsaturated stays liquid (fish omega-3, seed-oil omega-6); the answer names a fat family from how it acts. T3b (technique payoff): chefs deep-fry in high-smoke-point fats (tallow, refined oils) and save fragile extra-virgin olive oil as a finishing drizzle, because heat past the smoke point wrecks a fat. T4: the body needs both omega-3 (fatty fish — salmon, sardines) and omega-6 (seed oils), but the modern diet runs roughly 15-17x more omega-6 than omega-3 when older diets were near 1:1 — the fix is more oily fish, not fat-phobia. T5 (the debate, no verdict): 'seed oils' (soybean, corn, canola) are industrially extracted and very high in omega-6 linoleic acid; traditional-foods critics argue repeated heating oxidizes these fragile fats into harmful compounds and favor butter/tallow/olive oil, while the American Heart Association points to trials where swapping saturated fat for these oils improved heart markers — the honest answer names the actual crux (processing + oxidation + omega-6 excess), not a winner.
source: AHA 'No reason to avoid seed oils' (2024) & Presidential Advisory on dietary fats (Circulation); PMC6247292 (omega-6 controversies); ACS ChemMatters 'Seed Oils'; traditional-foods skeptic literature (oxidation/OXLAMs, omega-6:3 ratio); NIH ODS on fat-soluble vitamins. Grokipedia attempted (403).
framing_note: Scene-led; answers are foods, fat families, or the crux of the argument. Dinner-test payoff: T5 (the seed-oil fight is really about oxidation + omega-6:3 balance + processing, NOT 'fat is bad'). ACCURACY RAILS: present the seed-oil question as GENUINELY contested — human RCTs favor PUFA for heart markers, so do NOT assert seed oils are 'proven toxic'; steel-man BOTH sides; the tested answer is always the mechanism/crux, never a policy verdict. 'Brain is 60% fat' = by dry weight — phrase carefully. Contested-debate topic → vision_mandated true.

name: The Mediterranean pattern — and the detective story behind it
strand: Building a diet that fits your goals
scope: The most-praised traditional diet, and the science that made it famous. T2: the 'Mediterranean diet' everyone recommends is really a 1950s-60s peasant pattern from southern Italy, Greece and Crete — vegetables, beans, bread, fish, and the signature fat that defines it, olive oil, with little red meat or sugar (the answer is the olive oil). T3 (origin): it came from a real detective story — American scientist Ancel Keys noticed poor Mediterranean villagers had far LESS heart disease than well-fed Americans and launched the 'Seven Countries Study' to compare their diets; the finding was that the olive-oil-and-fish eaters had less heart disease than the steak-and-butter eaters. T4: its strength is the whole PATTERN, not one magic food — olive oil instead of butter, fish instead of red meat, and the part everyone forgets: piles of vegetables and legumes (plus daily walking and shared meals). T5 (contested): Keys' work also launched the 'saturated fat causes heart disease' idea that shaped 50 years of low-fat advice — a leap now heavily re-examined, since his study showed correlation, not proof, and his cohort selection is criticized; the diet pattern holds up, the anti-saturated-fat verdict is disputed.
source: MDPI Rev Cardiovasc Med 2025 'Ancel Keys, the Mediterranean Diet, and the Seven Countries Study: A Review' (PMC12027923); SevenCountriesStudy.com; PubMed 29134858 (Keys legacy); ongoing saturated-fat-hypothesis critique literature. Grokipedia attempted (403).
framing_note: Scene-led; keep the FOOD as the anchor (olive oil, fish, beans) and Keys as context — never make a bare human name the answer; T3's answer is the FINDING (villagers had less heart disease), not 'Ancel Keys'. Dinner-test payoff: T5 (the diet is well-supported but 'saturated fat is the villain' is contested). ACCURACY RAILS: no anachronism issue (mid-20th-c pattern, tomatoes fine); do NOT flip into 'Keys was a fraud' — that's the opposite strawman; steel-man both. Contested science on T5 → vision_mandated true.

name: Blue Zones — the longevity places, and the fraud twist
strand: Building a diet that fits your goals
scope: The five famous 'live-to-100' regions, their shared foods, and the honest skepticism. T2: 'Blue Zones' are five places researchers claimed have unusual numbers of 100-year-olds — Okinawa (Japan), Sardinia (Italy), Ikaria (Greece), Nicoya (Costa Rica), and Loma Linda (California); the Okinawan diet's old staple wasn't white rice but the purple SWEET POTATO. T3 (the shared food): one thing runs through nearly every Blue-Zone plate — a daily cup of beans/legumes (Sardinian fava, Nicoyan black beans, Okinawan soy); that's the common thread. T4: Loma Linda's long-lived group are Seventh-day Adventists who eat a handful of nuts most days and largely skip alcohol and tobacco — a sign it's a whole lifestyle, not one superfood (answer: the daily handful of nuts). T5 (the twist): in 2024 demographer Saul Newman won an Ig Nobel showing much Blue-Zone longevity data is shaky — the 'oldest' regions often had no birth certificates, high poverty, and pension-fraud incentives to overstate age, with birthdays clustering on suspicious round numbers; the food lessons (beans, vegetables, less junk) may still hold, but the 'magic longevity' claim is contested.
source: Blue Zones (Buettner) original framing; UCL news + Al Jazeera + Fortune + IFLScience coverage of Saul Newman's Ig Nobel 2024 work; bioRxiv 704080v3 (Newman, supercentenarian data/pension-fraud patterns); Buettner rebuttal. Grokipedia attempted (403).
framing_note: Scene-led; T2-T4 answers are concrete FOODS (sweet potato, beans, nuts) so the ladder earns its food-anchor even on a lifestyle topic. Dinner-test payoff: T5 (the age records are unreliable — pension fraud & missing birth certificates). ACCURACY RAIL: present BOTH Newman's critique AND that Buettner disputes it; do not moralize or dunk — the tone is honest curiosity. Contested claims → vision_mandated true.

name: Weston Price and the traditional-foods idea
strand: Building a diet that fits your goals
scope: The dentist who mapped what old diets did right. T2 (scene): in the 1930s a Cleveland dentist, Weston A. Price, traveled to isolated peoples — Swiss Alpine villages, Scottish islands, African tribes, Pacific islanders — and found that those eating their old traditional diets had near-perfect teeth and almost no cavities, until white flour and sugar arrived and their teeth began to rot (answer: their teeth decayed once modern flour/sugar came in). T3: the healthiest groups all prized certain 'sacred' foods rich in fat-soluble vitamins — organ meats, fish eggs, shellfish, and deep-yellow butter from cows on fast-growing spring grass. T4 (payoff): Price found a mystery nutrient in those foods, more powerful than vitamins A and D at building strong bones and teeth, and named it 'Activator X'; decades later (2007) it was identified as vitamin K2, which steers calcium into bones and teeth and away from arteries. T5: this is the root of the modern traditional-foods movement — fermented foods (sauerkraut, natto, yogurt), bone broth, whole-fat dairy, and soaked or soured grains; the honest caveat is Price's evidence was observational travel fieldwork, not controlled trials.
source: Weston A. Price Foundation (Activator X = vitamin K2 MK-4, identified 2007 by Chris Masterjohn/Sally Fallon); Price, 'Nutrition and Physical Degeneration' (1939); Dr. Steven Lin 'Mystery of Activator X'; K2 physiology literature. Grokipedia attempted (403).
framing_note: Scene-led; the FOODS are the anchor (spring butter, organ meats, natto, ferments) and Price is context. Dinner-test payoff: T4 (Activator X turned out to be vitamin K2). ACCURACY RAIL: be honest that Price's fieldwork was OBSERVATIONAL and some conclusions are debated — celebrate the core insight (whole traditional foods beat white-flour-and-sugar) without overclaiming. Traditional-foods advocacy → vision_mandated true; do not strawman mainstream nutrition.

name: Carbohydrates — smart vs empty, fiber, and blood sugar
strand: Building a diet that fits your goals
scope: Why not all carbs behave alike. T1 (scene): a whole apple and a glass of apple juice hold about the same sugar, yet the apple barely spikes you and the juice does — the difference is the one thing the whole food keeps: fiber, which slows the sugar's release. T2: 'refined' grains (white flour, white rice) have had the bran and germ stripped off — exactly the parts holding the fiber, vitamins and minerals — leaving mostly starch (that's what 'refined' removes). T3 (payoff): fiber isn't digested by YOU at all — it travels to your gut, where trillions of bacteria ferment it into compounds that feed and protect your colon lining. T4: a pile of sugar or white bread sends blood glucose up fast, triggering an insulin surge and a crash that leaves you hungry again within an hour — pairing carbs with protein, fat or fiber blunts the spike (that's why cereal alone leaves you starving mid-morning).
source: Harvard Nutrition Source (Carbohydrates, Fiber, whole vs refined grains); NIH/NIDDK on glycemic response & insulin; gut-microbiome fiber-fermentation literature (short-chain fatty acids). Grokipedia attempted (403).
framing_note: Scene-led; answers are the mechanism or the food part (fiber, bran+germ, gut bacteria). Dinner-test payoff: T3 (fiber feeds your gut bacteria, not you) — this quietly bridges to the fermentation strand. ACCURACY RAIL: whole-food lean is fine and settled here, but do NOT demonize all carbs — a whole potato, oats and fruit are good foods; the villain is the refined/empty version, not the macro. Settled physiology → vision_mandated false.

name: The vitamin hunt — deficiency diseases and the foods that cured them
strand: Building a diet that fits your goals
scope: Keystone food-history thread: one deadly deficiency + the specific food that fixes it, per rung. T2 (scurvy): on months-long voyages sailors' gums bled, teeth loosened and old wounds reopened — scurvy killed more men than battle, and the cure was a food: citrus (oranges, lemons). T3: in 1747 naval surgeon James Lind ran one of history's first controlled experiments, giving scurvy patients six different remedies — only the pair fed oranges and lemons recovered. T4 (the twist): Britain later switched from lemons to LIMES (grown in its own colonies) and scurvy quietly crept back, because limes carry only about half the vitamin C and it degraded further in storage — the cure was accidentally weakened even as the nickname 'limey' stuck. T4b (beriberi): sailors and city-dwellers eating polished WHITE rice grew weak and paralyzed; the missing piece was the very part milling removed — the rice bran/husk (thiamine), and Japanese navy doctor Takaki beat it by adding barley, meat and vegetables. T5 (pellagra): the corn-eating American South was ravaged by pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia, death), yet Mexicans eating even MORE corn stayed well — because they soak corn in lime/ash (nixtamalization), which unlocks the niacin bound inside the corn; the South skipped that step. T5b (goiter): swollen thyroid 'goiter' afflicted ~30% of the Great Lakes 'goiter belt' until a trace mineral was added to salt — iodine; within a decade of iodized salt (1924) it nearly vanished.
source: Wikipedia + Britannica + Science History Institute (James Lind 1747/publ.1753, citrus, limey, lime<lemon vitamin C); Wikipedia Takaki Kanehiro + Atlas Obscura 'Killer Rice' + Nobel (Eijkman) for beriberi/thiamine; Wikipedia Pellagra & Nixtamalization + Goldberger history; Healio + J. Nutrition (David Marine) on iodized salt 1924 Michigan, ~30%→<2% goiter. Grokipedia attempted (403).
framing_note: Scene-led, invert the wonder (lead with the deadly mystery, make the FOOD the knowable answer). One coherent theme (a deficiency + the food/food-process that cures it); the scientist is always context, never the answer. Dinner-test payoffs: T4 (limes were worse than lemons) and T5 (nixtamalization — soaking corn in lime unlocks niacin). ACCURACY RAILS: Lind 1747 (published 1753); Takaki's 1880s fix PREDATES the vitamin theory (don't credit him with discovering thiamine); nixtamalization is Mesoamerican (lime/wood-ash); iodized salt 1924, Michigan. Settled history/science → vision_mandated false.

name: Hydration — water, electrolytes, and the myths
strand: Building a diet that fits your goals
scope: Where water really comes from and what sweat really costs you. T2 (invert): you don't get water only from the tap — about a fifth of your daily water comes from FOOD, and some 'solid' foods are almost entirely water (a cucumber is ~97% water; watermelon and oranges over 90%; even a steak is ~65%). T3 (myth-buster): the famous 'drink 8 glasses a day' rule has no science behind it — it traces to a misread 1945 report that recommended ~2.5 liters total and then noted most of that is already in your food. T4 (payoff): when you sweat hard you lose more than water — you lose salt, and sodium is the main electrolyte in sweat (roughly a gram per liter); chugging only plain water after heavy sweating can leave you low on sodium, which is why athletes reach for electrolytes, not just water.
source: Harvard Health 'Using food to stay hydrated' (~20% from food); Tufts/Michigan Medicine debunking the 8x8 rule (1945 Food & Nutrition Board report); Precision Hydration + AHA on sweat sodium (~1 g/L) and electrolyte replacement. Grokipedia attempted (403).
framing_note: Scene-led; answers are foods, the myth's real origin, or the missing electrolyte. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (the 8-glasses rule is a misread report — food already supplies much of it). ACCURACY RAIL: don't over-scare — the point is 'plain water isn't the whole story', not that water is dangerous; sodium-isn't-the-enemy fits the traditional lean and is well-supported. Settled/myth-busting → vision_mandated false.

name: Eating for energy vs growth vs recovery
strand: Building a diet that fits your goals
scope: The same foods, aimed at different jobs. T2 (scene): your body runs on two main fuels — carbs for fast, hard effort (a sprint) and fat for slow all-day endurance; a marathoner 'hits the wall' near mile 20 when the fast fuel runs out — the stored carbohydrate (glycogen) — and is forced down to fat-burning pace. T3 (growth): for building a body — a kid in a growth spurt, a healing broken bone — the key is protein plus enough total calories and bone minerals (calcium, and vitamin D to use it); under-eating stalls growth. T4 (recovery): after hard exercise, muscle rebuilds best when you eat protein (the leucine trigger from the protein ladder) fairly soon after, alongside carbs to reload the glycogen you burned. T5 (payoff, ties the strand): this is why one plate doesn't fit everyone — an endurance athlete carb-loads before a race, a growing teen needs extra protein and calories, a person sitting all day needs fewer carbs; the foods are the same, the ratios change with the goal.
source: Sports-nutrition consensus (glycogen depletion / 'the wall'); Examine.com & pediatric sports-nutrition guidance (protein + calories for growth, calcium/vitamin D for bone); post-exercise protein+carb recovery literature. Grokipedia attempted (403).
framing_note: Scene-led; answers are the fuel or nutrient tied to the goal (glycogen, protein+carbs, adjust-the-ratio). Dinner-test payoff: T2 (the marathoner's 'wall' is running out of stored carbohydrate). ACCURACY RAIL: the post-workout 'anabolic window' is looser than gym lore claims — say 'fairly soon,' not a strict 30-minute deadline. Settled sports nutrition → vision_mandated false; T5 sets up the capstone tailoring ladder.

name: Food is information — tailoring the diet to your goal
strand: Building a diet that fits your goals
scope: Capstone: food is more than calories — it's signals your body reads. T3 (scene): 200 calories of eggs and 200 calories of soda do completely different things to your appetite — protein and fat trip fullness signals, while sugar spikes then crashes and leaves you hungry, so 'a calorie' isn't the same for hunger. T4 (payoff): the 'protein leverage' idea — your appetite hunts for a protein target, so when food is protein-poor (chips, soda) you keep eating and overshoot on total calories chasing the protein you need; protein-rich meals satisfy on fewer calories. T5 (the debate, no verdict): this sits inside a real argument — the mainstream 'energy balance' view says weight is mostly calories-in vs calories-out (a calorie is a calorie), while the challenger view says WHAT you eat shifts hormones (like insulin), hunger and how the body uses those calories; the honest answer names the actual crux — both camps agree calories matter, they disagree on whether food QUALITY changes appetite and metabolism enough to matter more.
source: Wikipedia + PMC10475875 (Protein Leverage Hypothesis, Simpson & Raubenheimer); satiety-hormone literature (ghrelin, CCK, GLP-1 responses to protein vs carb); carbohydrate-insulin model vs energy-balance model debate. Grokipedia attempted (403).
framing_note: Scene-led; the tested answer is a concept/crux, never a verdict. Dinner-test payoff: T4 (low-protein food makes you overeat because appetite chases protein). ACCURACY RAILS: steel-man BOTH the energy-balance and food-quality/insulin camps — do not declare a winner; protein-leverage is a well-supported hypothesis, not a proven law. This is the strand's capstone ('build a diet that fits YOUR goals') → contested framing, vision_mandated true.

name: Ultra-processed food — why it makes you overeat
strand: Building a diet that fits your goals
scope: The modern 'empty calories' problem, with the landmark experiment as payoff. T3 (scene): 'ultra-processed' isn't just any processing (freezing peas, canning beans is fine) — it means industrial formulations built from ingredients you'd never keep in a kitchen (emulsifiers, dyes, protein isolates, flavor blends); given a can of beans, frozen peas, and a neon breakfast cereal, the ultra-processed one is the cereal. T4 (payoff): in a 2019 NIH experiment (Kevin Hall), people were fed meals matched for calories, sugar, fat, salt AND fiber — yet on the ultra-processed menu they ate about 500 extra calories a day and gained weight, on the minimally-processed one they lost it. T5: the leading explanation is that ultra-processed food is engineered to be eaten FAST and soft and calorie-dense, and low in the protein/fiber that signal fullness — so the gut's 'stop eating' hormones can't keep up (people ate the ultra-processed food many calories-per-minute faster).
source: NIH news + Cell Metabolism 2019 (Hall et al., ad-libitum UPF RCT, ~+500 kcal/day, n=20); Chris van Tulleken 'Ultra-Processed People'; NOVA classification (Monteiro, Sao Paulo). Grokipedia attempted (403).
framing_note: Scene-led; answers are a food (the cereal), the experiment's result, or the mechanism (engineered to bypass fullness). Dinner-test payoff: T4 (matched for everything, people STILL overate ~500 cal on ultra-processed food). ACCURACY RAILS: the 'ultra-processed' (NOVA) category is itself debated and fuzzy — some ultra-processed foods aren't harmful, and Hall 2019 was one small (n=20) but landmark trial; present the lean-skeptical view honestly, not as settled dogma. The exact 500 number is context, the concept is tested. Contested definition → vision_mandated true.
